title: The Disputed Birthday Party
scenario_text: Two close friends, Alex and Blair, ask you to settle a fight. Alex spent two months and roughly $500 secretly planning a surprise birthday party for Blair's partner. Cake, decorations, fifteen guests invited, the partner's favorite restaurant booked out. The day before the party, Blair found out and canceled it. Their reason: the partner had been sick all week and Blair knew they wouldn't enjoy a crowd of people. Blair did not refund Alex for any of the costs. Alex is hurt and out of pocket. Alex says: 'I did all this for your partner, and you didn't even consult me before pulling the plug or offer to share the costs.' Blair says: 'You planned a major event involving my partner without checking with me first. That's on you.' They've asked you to rule. They will both accept your decision if your reasoning is sound.
framing_note: Adjudication requires a decision. 'They're both wrong' and 'they're both right' aren't rulings. You'll need to identify who is mostly in the wrong, what principle your ruling rests on, and why the losing side's argument — which is real — doesn't carry the day. Imagine you'll have to defend your reasoning to both of them.

user_options.label: I'll rule for Alex
user_options.position: Blair is mostly in the wrong; Alex is owed at minimum a partial reimbursement and an apology

user_options.label: I'll rule for Blair
user_options.position: Alex is mostly in the wrong; Blair owes nothing because Alex assumed the risk by not consulting them

user_options.label: I'll rule for a split obligation
user_options.position: Both are partly in the wrong; here is how I would divide the obligation between them

evaluation_criteria: Did the user actually rule, or did they evade ('they're both wrong')?
Did the user articulate a clear principle that the ruling rests on, not just an opinion about the case?
Does the principle generalize — would it produce a sensible answer if the facts changed slightly?
Did the user acknowledge the losing side's strongest argument and explain why it loses here, rather than dismissing it?
Did the user distinguish 'wrong' from 'owes a remedy' (sophisticated adjudication often separates these)?
ai_focus_hints: If the user says 'they're both equally wrong' or 'I can't decide', refuse it gently but firmly: 'That's the easy answer. If I forced you to lean one way, even slightly, which way and why?' Adjudication requires a decision.
If the user picks a side without articulating a principle, push: 'What's the rule you're applying? If I changed the facts, would the same rule produce the same answer?'

If the user's principle is too narrow ('A should have asked because the partner was sick'), push: 'Would A still need to ask if the partner wasn't sick? Is your rule about asking, or about something else?'
If the user dismisses the losing side's case, force engagement: 'They have a real point. Why isn't it enough?'

Try at most ONE fact-tweak per session. Suggested tweaks: 'What if the costs were $50 not $500?' or 'What if Blair had said weeks ago they liked surprises?' or 'Would your rule still feel right if it were applied to YOU next time you planned something for a friend?' One variable, fairly tested.

Concede genuinely when the user states a clear principle that holds under one fact-tweak, acknowledges the losing side's strongest point honestly, and gives reasoning both parties could accept. That's real adjudication.
wrap_trigger: Wrap when the user has issued a ruling, articulated the supporting principle, and survived at least one principle-test hypothetical without abandoning their reasoning. If the user keeps refusing to rule, do not wrap — keep the pressure on gently. The exercise is incomplete without a decision.
